video.title: I've Started 75+ Businesses: Here’s What Actually Matters

summary: Chris Koerner looks back on businesses he started over 15 years and uses them to explain how a small-business CEO should handle operations, people, capital, focus, and risk. The examples include iPhone repair, LCD Cycle, online bread sales, e-commerce food fulfilment, Bitcoin mining, RV and mobile-home parks, and tree trimming. He emphasizes learning how the work is done before delegating, protecting employees and company culture, and checking partners and deals carefully. His cautionary examples show that fast growth and attractive spreadsheets can hide weak margins, concentration risk, or poor partner fit.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: The Koerner Office host; the video is a solo career and business lessons presentation.

ideas.name: Phone Restore iPhone repair stores
ideas.one_liner: A walk-in iPhone repair business that grew from a college storefront to multiple locations and tested a mall kiosk.
ideas.business_model: Repair services; the specific pricing model was not stated.
ideas.customer: People with broken iPhones, including college students.
ideas.offer: In-person iPhone repairs from storefronts and a mall kiosk. The founder learned repairs as customers arrived.

pricing.notes: No repair price was stated. The $600 figure refers to a customer's phone, not the repair charge.

acquisition_channels.details: He put an advertisement on wristbands and distributed them to college bars. Students who broke their phones returned with the advertised wristband.

quote.text: I ordered a few boxes of them. I distributed them to bars. College students would go to the bar, break their iPhone, get drunk, wake up, broke an iPhone and a wristband with an ad on it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: A storefront next to a Subway relied on people walking in. A mall kiosk was tested for its walk-through traffic.

quote.text: I wanted to see could we have an iPhone repair kiosk. Is that a thing? I hadn't seen it which made me nervous but I thought there's a lot of walk walkth through traffic.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: After tornado damage, he put up a sign at the damaged store and says people felt bad for them and made purchases.

quote.text: So, we went to Home Depot, put this sign up. People felt bad for us. We got some sales.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: After the tornadoes, he listed phones bought back from customers that had not yet been listed on eBay. This generated cash from inventory rather than repair bookings.

quote.text: And we had a bunch of iPhones that we had bought back from customers that we had never listed on eBay. So, we thought, "Okay, let's list those on eBay."
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Repairs were performed in person. The founder initially learned how to repair each customer's phone using YouTube, then later ran stores and a kiosk. A repair mistake damaged a customer's phone and caused data loss.
unit_economics_claims: The business grew to four locations before it was sold.
The founder says two-cent wristbands were used for local advertising.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The founder signed a lease with a personal guarantee; wristbands cost two cents each.

acquisition.how: Store foot traffic, local bar wristband distribution, and a physical sign require local presence and coordination. A website or paid advertising could supplement these channels, but neither was described.

onboarding.how: A customer brings in a device and staff assess it. The transcript describes a walk-in interaction, not automated intake.

delivery.how: A person must physically diagnose and repair each phone.

billing.how: The transcript does not explain payment or invoicing; an online point-of-sale system could handle routine charges, with staff resolving exceptions.

support.how: Questions and device problems require human judgement, especially where a repair damages a device or data.

uk_applicability.notes: The local repair-store model and venue-based advertising can work in the UK. The described inbound walk-in strategy does not rely on unsolicited electronic marketing.

risks: A personal lease guarantee created personal exposure.
The founder initially accepted repair jobs before knowing how to do them, creating stressful customer experiences.
A punctured battery produced smoke, and the customer lost data and had to receive a replacement phone.
A tornado destroyed part of the store and overnight revenue fell to zero.
A trusted employee stole phones and cash, according to the founder.
The mall kiosk test involved physical battery repairs and customer property, so an error could be costly.

ideas.problem: Chris thought the bread was not available online and that this limited its sales.
ideas.offer: Set up online sales for Hartland Bread and receive a cut of what sold online.

pricing.notes: The commission rate and bread prices were not stated.

acquisition_channels.details: The bread was sold online, but the transcript does not say how online customers were acquired.

ideas.delivery: Chris said he would handle and pay for the online sales effort. The bakery made the bread; the transcript does not explain order fulfilment or shipping.
ideas.startup_cost: Chris offered to pay for the online launch; the amount was not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Chris says the online sales effort worked and that sales increased during COVID.

ideas.name: Send Eats e-commerce food fulfilment
ideas.one_liner: A warehouse logistics business fulfilling orders for e-commerce food brands.
ideas.business_model: Fulfilment and logistics service for food brands; specific fees and billing basis were not stated.
ideas.customer: E-commerce food brands. Chris says one customer accounted for most of the company's revenue and employee workload.
ideas.problem: Food brands selling online needed a logistics and fulfilment provider.
ideas.offer: A warehouse operation to fulfil e-commerce food orders.

pricing.notes: The transcript states monthly top-line revenue but not the prices charged to customers.

acquisition_channels.details: Chris says he took sales calls, but does not explain how prospects were sourced. The 80% close-rate example is discussed during the Bitcoin mining period and is not attributed to Send Eats.

ideas.delivery: A 10,000-square-foot warehouse and 32 employees fulfilled customer orders. Chris describes the business as low margin and says the largest customer drove much of the workload.
unit_economics_claims: The business reached $300,000 in monthly top-line revenue but was not profitable.
One customer represented 85% of revenue and 85% of employees' work.
Chris later described that customer as paying $250,000 per month in unprofitable top-line revenue.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Chris says the company signed a lease on a 10,000-square-foot warehouse.

acquisition.how: B2B prospecting and sales could use software, but the transcript gives no repeatable lead source. UK cold email must target limited companies, and cold calls must screen TPS and CTPS.

onboarding.how: Customer inventory and order integrations could automate routine setup, but onboarding food brands and resolving data or product issues would need human oversight.

delivery.how: Physical goods have to be received, stored, picked, packed, and shipped by people or machines in a warehouse.

billing.how: A fulfilment platform could calculate routine charges from order and storage data, with human review for exceptions. No billing system was described.

support.how: Customer service and fulfilment problems require human coordination, especially for a concentrated, high-value account.

uk_applicability.notes: E-commerce fulfilment can operate in the UK, with adjustments for food handling, labelling, shipping, and UK tax rules. The transcript's low-margin competition and customer concentration would also apply.

risks: The business had a large warehouse lease and many employees, creating fixed costs.
Chris says monthly revenue sounded attractive but the company was not profitable.
He says the business was low margin and competed with Amazon while sitting between mass-market and expensive niche fulfilment.
A single customer accounted for 85% of revenue and most of the employee workload.
The customer was toxic, and ending the relationship required dismissing employees as well as firing the account.

tactics.name: Learn the work by doing it
steps: Start by understanding the actual customer work and the decisions staff make.
At Phone Restore, Chris accepted repair jobs and learned from YouTube when the customer left.
For tree trimming, learn how to quote jobs, talk to subcontractors, and set target gross margins.
Use that knowledge to delegate later rather than staying in every task forever.

quote.text: You don't need to stay in the weeds, but you got to start in the weeds. For instance, in my we have we own a tree trimming business.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use a specific low-cost local promotion
steps: Identify where the target customers gather.
Put the repair-shop advertisement on custom wristbands costing two cents each.
Distribute them to bars so students see the offer when they wake up with a broken phone.

quote.text: I Googled custom wristbands. They were 2 cents each. I ordered a few boxes of them. I distributed them to bars.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Test a new location with a short commitment
steps: Notice foot traffic that could support a new format.
Test a mall kiosk rather than assuming it will work.
Use a month-to-month lease so the location can be cancelled if demand is insufficient.

quote.text: You know it's monthto month so if it doesn't work out we can cancel it. So crazy story.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Turn stranded inventory into cash during a disruption
steps: When the store lost revenue after the tornado, look for inventory that could be sold through another channel.
List the customer buy-back iPhones that had not yet been posted on eBay.

quote.text: And we had a bunch of iPhones that we had bought back from customers that we had never listed on eBay. So, we thought, "Okay, let's list those on eBay."
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Build an online sales channel on a low-risk revenue share
steps: Find a good product that is not available online.
Offer to create and fund the online sales channel.
Agree to receive a cut of online sales if the channel works, with no charge to the supplier if it fails.

quote.text: I'll do everything. I'll pay for it. If it works, give me a cut of everything I sell online. If it doesn't, no harm, no foul.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Check whether growth is profitable
steps: Separate top-line revenue from profit when evaluating a business.
Include warehousing, labour, and customer concentration in the operating picture.
Do not let a large monthly revenue figure substitute for margin analysis.

quote.text: We were making 300 grand a month. Asterisk topline, not profitable. Didn't know it at the time.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Reduce customer concentration by winning more accounts
steps: Keep serving a large customer well rather than firing it solely because it is a large share of revenue.
Continue acquiring other customers to reduce the concentration over time.
Check whether the account is profitable and whether its behaviour is damaging the team.

quote.text: You just take great care of the customer and you try to get more to drop the 85%.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Do partner diligence before committing
steps: Check a prospective partner's character and history as well as their industry knowledge.
Investigate whether they have a pattern of pushing partners out.
Use calculated pressure and deliberate diligence before moving quickly into a deal.

quote.text: I knew that they knew the industry. I didn't know their character. Looking back, I'm grateful for that experience.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Protect strong employees and company culture
steps: Address a toxic employee when they are making strong contributors leave.
Check in with high-performing managers and employees instead of assuming they will remain engaged.
Proactively recognize and reward strong employees before they ask for a raise.

quote.text: If your rockstar employee has asked you for a raise, you're probably too late. Your rockstar employee should not have to come to you.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Develop the habit of finding a workable next step when a problem appears, rather than stopping at 'I can't do it.'

quote.text: The make it happen gene is just the ability to say everything is figure outable. And the inability to ever just throw your hands up and just say I can't do it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Learn the operational details before delegating, then step out of the work so the business can scale.

quote.text: You don't need to stay in the weeds, but you got to start in the weeds.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: A small, specific experiment can reveal a customer acquisition channel that desk research would miss.

quote.text: And so I pulled out my Dell laptop. I Googled custom wristbands. They were 2 cents each.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: A CEO should absorb difficult business problems and protect employees from avoidable stress.

quote.text: And it is your job, it is your role to insulate everyone else from that because they're W2 employees.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Capital helps a business grow, but the terms and the source of advice matter; seek advice from people who have your interests in mind.

quote.text: Capital is fuel and if you run out of it, you run out of your business.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Distinguish revenue from profit and inspect margins before treating growth as success.

quote.text: We were making 300 grand a month. Asterisk topline, not profitable. Didn't know it at the time.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Learn a partner's character and history, not only their industry expertise.

quote.text: I knew that they knew the industry. I didn't know their character.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Give strong employees regular attention and recognition; do not assume they will stay engaged without it.

quote.text: If your rockstar employee has asked you for a raise, you're probably too late.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: When a major customer is harmful to the team, weigh the revenue against the effect on employees and the company's culture.

quote.text: You have to take care of yourself and your own mental health or else your employees will suffer from you or they will suffer from your toxic customer.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: A business can be growing quickly at a moment of favourable timing; do not assume the same results will persist.

quote.text: I lucked out. I found this facility offmarket, undermarket. We bought it. We felt like geniuses. Absolute geniuses.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: A CEO can delegate work, but still needs to check in with strong operators and invest in their success.

quote.text: You still got to touch base. You've got to know the weeds.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

evidence_quality.rationale: Chris speaks about businesses he says he started and gives specific examples of operations, customer acquisition, financing, and growth. Many financial outcomes are self-reported, some figures are described without context, and the transcript does not provide records to verify them.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host promotes his free videos and asks viewers to subscribe. No paid sponsor or course sale is stated.
